title: OPP officers tell their stories of recovering from PTSD
subtitle: Not all officers suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder complain of the treatment they received from their employer.
article: Not all OPP officers who suffered post-traumatic stress disorder have harrowing tales to tell Ontario Ombudsman Andre Marin of a police force that doesn't take PTSD seriously.
Three OPP officers and one civilian say they have recovered from the disorder and are once again thriving professionally.
"I got a second chance at life," says OPP Const. Garry Mellan, 49.
He lost his wife, his kids, his home and his job when he became an emotional mess after killing a man in a gunfight in 1996 in Cat Lake, First Nations.
He also thought he'd lost his marbles.
The lowest point, he says, was when the sound of firecrackers on Canada Day gave him such anxiety one year that he dropped into the fetal position on his bathroom floor and began weeping.
However, the OPP were willing to reassign him, and he's now a crime analyst at the East Region headquarters in Smiths Falls, Ont.
Others tell similar stories.
• OPP officer Brad Hollywood, now 46, shot and killed Jason Steacy, 20, following a minor stabbing on Nov. 4, 2005.
He was off for six weeks recovering.
"The OPP told me take as much as you need until you're feeling strong," Hollywood said.
Hollywood said the most important part is to accept that the event will have an impact, and to reach out and ask for support or accept support if it is offered.
He is now a sergeant in the provincial communications unit at Smiths Falls.
• OPP Sgt. Brian Eadie, 53, was himself close to death on June 9, 2008 from attending a suicide call at a house in Martintown, near Cornwall.
He works out of the Stormont, Dundas & Glengarry detachment in Long Sault, Ont.
On that night in 2008, Mathew McNaughton, 28, who was suicidal, threw a Molotov cocktail at Eadie and his partner, Const. Jeremy Falle.

The front hallway of the house exploded and their bodies were engulfed in flames. They were trapped because the front door had slammed shut because of the explosion. Falle shot out the front glass, and they crawled through the window.
"He saved my life," Eadie says.
McNaughton later died in a burn unit, while Eadie suffered severe burns to his face and hands, back and legs.
Throughout the summer, Eadie's burns began healing quite well, but something he didn't recognize was going on in his head.
He was getting depressed and was filled with guilt over the death of the man he had come to save.
"I had a lot of bad dreams, trouble sleeping," Eadie says.
After receiving counselling, he returned to work in June 2009 and performed administrative duties for a year. By June, 2010, he asked to go back on the road.
Bad mistake.
One week later, he was working the midnight shift and was dispatched to two tractor trailers engulfed in flames on Highway 401 at Ingleside, Ont.
Two days later, the horror of that first night came back to haunt him.
"I started getting anxious. The old feelings came back, but they were worse this time," he said. "The smell of gasoline bothered me for a long time," he said.
After visiting the psychologist again, he realized that the truck accident reawakened the horrors of the Molotov cocktail that almost took his life.
He came back to work part-time in November, 2010 and, by February, 2011, he was back full time. He's been performing full administrative duties ever since.
"There is a good side to the OPP too," Eadie says.
• Sherry McCarthy, who is a call taker at the communications centre in Smiths Falls, won't forget May 17, 2007.
A call came through at 5:50 a.m., only an hour before her 12-hour shift was to end.
A woman was asking for help because her husband was drunk and yelling at her. McCarthy spoke to both of them and told the husband to wait outside for the officers.
Instead, however, he grabbed a knife and began stabbing her.
"Die, b--h," the man yelled while McCarthy was still on the phone. "I had to stay on the phone the whole time," McCarthy said.

When it was over, she ran out of the room and went to a dark corner and began crying. Without having slept or eaten, she returned that night for her next shift, but couldn't finish the shift and went home.
Her supervisor placed a call to the critical incident team and within an hour someone was there to talk to her.
She was off for three months to receive therapy.
McCarthy came back to work in a different part of the communications centre, but is now back performing her regular duties.
"We're often forgotten," she said of being a call taker and not an officer.
